graduation_requirements.raw_text:
Course Requirements
Students meet course requirements by achieving an overall course score that is in the proficient
range or above (2.6 or greater). Students can meet course requirements through course offerings, as
well as for a variety of different types of experiences that are aligned with one or more course
requirements (for more, see Flexible Pathways on page 7). Regardless of the pathway, students must
demonstrate proficiency in the following:

                 English                                 4 years
                 Social Studies                          3 years
                 Mathematics                             3 years
                 Science                                 3 years
                 Visual or Performing Arts               2 semesters or 1 year
                 Physical Education                      3 semesters
                 Health                                  1 semester
                 Electives                               4 learning opportunities
                 *Two years of the same World Language is recommended


Learning Expectation Requirement
Students meet the Learning Expectation requirement by achieving an overall score in each of the six
Learning Expectations that is in the proficient range or above (2.6 or greater) over the course of
their time at Harwood.

Learning Expectations
   1.​ Communication and Creative Expression - Express ideas and information clearly and
       creatively to reach a variety of audiences.
   2.​ Integrative Thinking - Create new meaning from evidence, multiple views, perspectives,
       opposing models, or seemingly unrelated ideas.
   3.​ Literacy - Read and write to develop the fundamental skills of critical thinking and an
       understanding of oneself and the world.
   4.​ Personal and Global Engagement - Contribute positively to a diverse culture that respects
       others, fosters responsibility, promotes personal wellness and embraces community and
       global awareness.
   5.​ Problem Solving - Interpret or define a problem and apply logic, rules, creativity and/or
       abstract thinking to find a solution.
   6.​ Self Direction - Make decisions and organize work independently rather than being told
       what to do by other people.

Community Service
Community service plays a vital role in the Harwood experience by specifically giving students the
opportunity to think of others and give back, creating a greater sense of belonging and involvement.
During the 2026-2027 school year all High School students grades 9-12 will be expected to
complete 10 hours of community service. Students will have many options and opportunities
throughout the year, including our annual fall Harvest Fest.

PLEASE NOTE:
   ●​ This expectation applies to all students grades 9-12 who take two or more classes AT
      Harwood.
   ●​ For students applying or in the National Honor Society these hours are in addition to the
      expectations of NHS.

courses.description: Windows and Mirrors, your 9th grade English class, begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate ourselves and others through a range of literature. We will learn how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, we will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, and use evidence, reasoning, and elaboration to support our thinking.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: In Sports and Adventure Literature, students will learn about themes that transcend specific texts, develop analytical and descriptive writing skills, understand the formal techniques and structure of sports and adventure texts and work individually and collaboratively to explore themes and techniques used by writers. Roughly one quarter will be dedicated to sports literature and the second quarter will focus on adventure literature.
courses.notes: Listed as an elective for grades 9-12 in the English department chart (semester).

courses.description: Intergenerational Book Club is a project-based class partnering Harwood students with seniors in the community to choose, read, and discuss books. The course is designed to build bridges across time and space, connecting young and more experienced community members around the acts of reading, talking, and writing about books. Students should expect to play an active role in their learning by designing, planning, and facilitating community bookgroup meetings. We will balance class time between working with books, corresponding with community partners, planning upcoming events, and reflecting on how we are meeting our goals.

What does it mean to be American? What are the values that we share versus the enduring tensions in our society? In this discussion-based course, students will study American fiction, non-fiction, poetry, and plays to better understand our nation and its heritage. We will examine the historical context of each piece that we read, and will often consider how the ideas of the authors speak to or contrast with current events.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: The primary goal of this semester-long English course is to become leaders in the design and practice of Harkness pedagogy and bring student-driven inquiry to the greater Harwood community. Just as important are the life skills you take away from this class, including honing your critical thinking (in reading, writing and reflection), public speaking, and ability to work as a team to innovate and problem solve.
courses.notes: Department chart lists it as an elective for grades 10, 11 and 12 (semester only); course entry states Grade: 10, 11.

courses.description: Why does news matter? In this course we explore its importance to democracy, its relationship to the First Amendment, and media ethics. This is a hands-on course; we will read and evaluate news in many forms, but we will also put out our own products in digital editions of “Common Ground,” photo essays, and podcasting. These pieces will reflect the interests of you, your classmates, and our greater Harwood community. The philosophy for our journalistic efforts can be summed up in one simple phrase: for students, by students, about things that students care about.

This year-long course is designed to build your creative writing and reading skills with a focus on creative nonfiction, short-fiction, and poetry. You will be asked to read, discuss, and analyze exemplary works of literature as well as create and respond to your own and your classmates’ work. In this class, you will explore a variety of ways to create meaningful pieces of writing. You will also have the opportunity to extend your audience beyond the classroom.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English OR a recommendation from a 9th grade English teacher
courses.notes: Department chart: requires teacher recommendation (10th grade).

courses.description: In this hands-on class, students will be actively learning how to write for business. They will analyze and write about business transactions as well as reading literature about famous businessmen and women and historical booms and collapses. We will look at socially responsible companies such as Ben & Jerry's and Darn Tough Socks Vermont and analyze their advertising and marketing communication through media literacy messaging.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of 10th grade English or a recommendation from 9th grade English teachers (10th graders)

courses.description: This semester-long course examines master storytellers of mystery fiction and the art and craft of writing mystery fiction in its many forms, including detective stories, thrillers, and suspense. The goal is to understand and model the concepts of adventure, keeping secrets, and high octane suspense. Students can expect to read, discuss, and write mystery fiction in this course.

How can ancient stories inform our world today? What commonalities do we see among combatants and non-combatants in the stories told across eras? War Stories begins with the foundational Western war story, Homer’s Iliad, and then follows war storytelling to contemporary society. In this course, we uncover the tragedy and glory of the Greeks’ epic battle with Troy and its parallels to contemporary warfare. Our materials include Stanley Lombardo’s translation of Iliad paired with Gareth Hinds’ graphic adaptation of it; Lysistrata, by Aristophanes; All Quiet on the Western Front, by Erich Marie Remarque; The Things They Carried, by Tim O’Brien; City of Thieves, by David Benioff, along with multiple short stories, excerpts, poetry, and films. Students are expected to take ownership of their own learning, do the work, and drive our classroom discussions and discoveries. We will look at our texts through six themes: courage and cowardice; women’s roles in war; old men say, young men do; brotherhood and bonds; good leadership/bad leadership; and honor and dishonor. With every source we read, view, or discuss, we will return to these themes. As an elective course, there will be LESS homework than a core content course, but do expect to read outside of class time. Be mindful that the course will read about and discuss difficult and mature content that is often uncomfortable.

Whose stories are worth telling? Which parts of our lives are important? In this Harkness-based course, we will read, discuss, and write about the work of women writers. We will explore a variety of poems, song lyrics, short fiction, essays, videos, and novels. Discover what women’s voices have to teach you, and develop your own voice as you consider their impact!

The AP English Language and Composition course aligns to an introductory college-level rhetoric and writing curriculum, which requires students to develop evidence-based analytic and argumentative essays. Students evaluate, synthesize and cite research to support their arguments. Throughout the course, students develop a personal style by making appropriate grammatical choices. Students also discover and analyze rhetorical elements in non-fiction texts from many disciplines including: speeches, biographies, contemporary non-fiction, business, sports, graphic images and historical periods. Students who take the AP English Language and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: This course is designed to replicate an introductory college-level literary analysis course. Its goal is to engage students in the close reading and critical analysis of imaginative literature, thereby deepening their understanding of the ways writers use language to provide both meaning and pleasure. The class is inquiry based and encourages students to delve deeply into the material, take ownership of their learning and drive our classroom discussions.In this course, students can expect to read novels, plays, short stories, and poetry, and discuss those works through student driven inquiry such as Harkness. Writing assignments include expository, analytical, and argumentative essays that require students to analyze and interpret literary works. Students who take the AP English Literature and Composition course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR a recommendation from an English teacher with a sample of literary analysis; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: The Global Studies experience begins with you, the student. What makes you unique, and how do you fit into your local and global communities? We will investigate our identities, our historical moment and how we got here, and how to use communication skills to create the change we want to see in the world. In this course, students will learn to closely read and analyze texts, participate in student-led discussions, write effectively, listen actively, conduct research, and use evidence and reasoning to support their own thinking. The goal of this course is to help students build communication, research, and critical thinking skills while developing their own sense of what it means to be a Global Citizen.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: What does it mean to be a citizen in a republic? In Three Democracies, we learn about the rise and fall of democracy in ancient Athens and Rome, making connections to the United States and the challenges that we face. Students consider timeless and timely questions about justice, leadership, political division, empire, and more. Importance is placed on applying lessons from the past to the present. This course features a combination of reading, reflection, discussion, projects, and writing.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
courses.notes: One of three 11th grade required options (Three Democracies, Creating Sustainable Communities, AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

courses.description: U.S. History helps students learn about the past events, peoples and ideas that make up the United States of America, from the Native American civilizations to the founding documents drafted in Pennsylvania to the Civil and the World Wars, always taking into account the rich and vibrant tapestry of people whose roots and culture hail from all over the world and thus contribute to the unique American story. Students will learn to research and evaluate evidence, including primary sources; they will learn how to put information and ideas into context and how to compare sources and various accounts of the past. Students work alone and together as they deepen their ability to read closely and annotate texts, engage in civil discourse, write short texts and longer essays, and create and teach each other with multimedia presentations. Finally, students will not only learn about the past; they will reflect on the issues facing the country in the present, always inspired by the question: “How does learning about the past help us better understand the present and make more informed choices about the future?” The course makes extensive use of primary and secondary readings, textbooks, and videos. Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
courses.fulfills_text: Successful completion of U.S. History is a graduation requirement.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: CSC is designed to help students understand how the U.S. political system really works (political literacy), how the media influences the political system (media literacy), how to develop and communicate an educated opinion on important public policies (critical literacy, argumentative writing, and civil discourse), and how to use the tools they have available to them to make change in their local and/or state-wide communities (action civics). Students should expect to do the following in this course: ●​ Analyze, mark-up, and annotate a variety of written and recorded texts and media sources ●​ Thoughtfully consider multiple perspectives through civil discourse, active listening, note-taking, and deliberative dialogue ●​ Communicate an educated opinion on a variety of current events and political issues ●​ Develop a plan for taking action on an issue they care deeply about and/or addressing a need in the community through active citizenship or social entrepreneurship This course is unique to Harwood Union High School. It is designed to be deeply relevant and responsive to both current events and student interest. The goal of this course is to help students become the type of citizens who are able to create more resilient, more equitable, more joyful, more just, and more sustainable communities, now and in the future.
courses.fulfills_text: REQUIRED course (11th grade): Three Democracies, or Creating Sustainable Communities, or AP U.S. Government
courses.notes: One of three 11th grade required options.

courses.description: Who are you? Why is your behavior similar to or different from other humans? Psychology is a social science that seeks to answer questions about human behavior and this course explores the latest, peer-reviewed research in an attempt to shed light on the mysterious world inside your head. In particular, we will explore what science has discovered about learning, memory, emotions, creativity, sensory perception, and much more. In the end, you’ll understand how your brain really works—and how to get the most out of it. Class activities, readings, and assignments are designed so students can reflect upon personal experiences and how psychology applies to all aspects of human life. Harkness dialogue and presentations are common summative assessments in this course. Psychology is a vastly broad topic encompassing a wide range of areas of study. Behavior, learning and memory, childhood development, language, and internal mental processes are just a few examples. Students should leave this course with an understanding of the brain and its processes, human behavior, the scientific method and ethics of experimentation, and the history and differing perspectives within the study of psychology.

Students will explore how advertising shapes culture, identity, and values — and how it can also promote health, well-being, and the common good. Through student inquiry and hands-on projects, students will learn to research, design, and launch media campaigns that make a positive social impact. Students will begin the semester by exploring how marketing and advertising have evolved over time before moving on to issues in contemporary media and advertising. Students will then work with a community partner to develop a media and marketing campaign, including some students who will work to “market” Harwood Union High School. Note: the idea for this course, as well as the curriculum, was co-created in collaboration with a number of current Harwood students who will also be serving as teaching assistants next year.

History on Film is a course where students view and analyze feature films and movies, documentaries, and other audio and visual media, along with printed source material. The purpose is to gain historical knowledge, ask probing questions, and develop an informed opinion on topics that increase one’s understanding about past, present, and future issues and events. The primary forms of assessment are film analysis and class discussions to evaluate student learning and understanding. Students will need to be comfortable respectfully sharing ideas, supported by evidence, within a large group. Other types of assessment include detailed film notes, written reflections, and individual and group projects and presentations.

This course explores major events and contemporary issues in the news, while seeking to understand how they have developed from a historical perspective. Students analyze news accounts in various sources: mainstream and more independent media, social media and other venues. Context is always important so the historical roots of these problems will be examined and questioned. As historians and critical media consumers we will also consider: What is the role of media in a democratic society? What makes the “news” and how do reporters and editors interpret events? Can we believe what we read, see, hear and “click”? Students will help guide the directions we take and we’ll look at and critically consider all of it: the mainstream TV channels and “newspapers,” credible “alternative” media outlets, original documents, social media, radio and podcasts and even some of the less-than credible sources, to make sure we understand how peoples’ ideas and opinions are shaped. Class activities are discussion-based, and students will be able to demonstrate their learning through class dialogue, reaction papers, original projects, and digital presentations.

Economic decisions impact our everyday lives. Understanding economics means thinking about how limited resources require us to make choices and evaluate one option against another. In this course, you will come to recognize that there are examples of economics all around you. You will see how these economic choices, from larger groups such as state and federal governments, to individual consumers, impact us every day. This course will examine the basic concepts of economics, the pros and cons of capitalism, communism, and socialism, the federal and state budget-making process, our growing national deficit, income inequality, the role of the government during a recession, as well as economics-related current events stories.

Street Law explores the laws in our streets, cities, and states. This course provides a general overview of law and the role that it plays in our society. Areas of focus include constitutional law, criminal law, civil rights, contract law, civil law, and family law. Students are given practical information, helpful in our law-saturated society. The textbook and the U.S. Constitution provide the basic framework for our understanding of laws. Current events provide realistic examples of how the law applies to human actions. Discussions and note-taking are expected, and student presentations on law-related topics are required. Students will also be expected to participate in a series of mock trials.

AP U.S. Government and Politics provides students with the skills and knowledge to be active citizens in our American Republic, as well as to prepare them for success in taking the AP Gov Exam. Students can expect to discuss current events, analyze graphs, write argumentative essays, complete projects, read Supreme Court cases, participate in Harkness discussions, and take practice AP Gov tests. One major goal in AP Gov is for students to learn about how our government is designed to operate in theory and to develop a clearer understanding of how it operates in practice.
courses.prerequisites: A 3.3 or higher in your current English class OR you may submit a written appeal to the History Department to take the course; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework
courses.fulfills_text: Counts as an 11th grade required option (AP U.S. Government with a U.S. History course score of 3.3 or greater).

courses.description: AP European History is a survey overview of the development of modern Europe. The time period covered by the course is 1450 - the present day. The following is taken from the College Board’s Course Description: AP European History is designed to be the equivalent of a two-semester introductory college or university European history course. In AP European History, students investigate significant events, individuals, developments, and processes in four historical periods from approximately 1450 to the present. Students develop and use the same skills, practices, and methods employed by historians: analyzing primary and secondary sources; developing historical arguments; making historical comparisons; and utilizing reasoning about contextualization, causation, and continuity and change over time. The course also provides six themes that students explore throughout the course in order to make connections among historical developments in different times and places: interaction of Europe and the world; poverty and prosperity; objective knowledge and subjective visions; states and other institutions of power; individual and society; and national and European identity. Students who take AP European History are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability, and trigonometry. Learn to find heights of tall objects. Explore problems about data. Solve problems using constraints. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Methods for writing and graphing linear equations ●​ And more! The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.

This course is designed for students who want to double up on math courses to provide additional challenges or to provide more opportunity for electives later in their high school career. This course addresses fundamental math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions, statistics and probability and trigonometry. These strands are unified in themed units and students will develop math habits of mind through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Algebraic fluency skills ●​ Using properties of similarity and trigonometry to solve problems ●​ Methods to collect, represent, and analyze data ●​ Probability & expected value The goal of this course is to give students a foundational understanding of algebra, trigonometry and statistics.
courses.prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an Quarter 3 course score of 3.3 or above in 8th grade math; Must successfully complete a set of online prerequisite tasks and a formative assessment. This will be assigned digitally in March and due in early April.; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period; Teacher recommendation will be considered in this decision
courses.notes: Must be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 (in person).

courses.description: This course addresses intermediate math concepts in the areas of algebra and functions and geometry. Explore exponents with Alice in Wonderland. Blast off some quadratic equations with fireworks. Maximize your geometric potential with the corrals unit. Students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Three forms of linear functions ●​ Methods for solving systems of equations ●​ Exponential relationships, properties of exponents, and logarithms ●​ Creation and transformation of quadratic functions to solve problems ●​ Surface area, volume, and trigonometry, and other elements of Euclidean geometry The goal of this course is to give students an intermediate understanding of algebra and geometry.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have a proficient course score in either Integrated Math 1 (or be concurrently enrolled in IM 1 online and meet the criteria for the online course)

courses.description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. This course is designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
courses.prerequisites: Must take this course concurrently with Integrated Math 2; Must have an overall course score of 3.3 or above in Integrated Math 1; Must have a self direction of 3.3 or above; Must have STAR score in the 70th percentile or higher in most recent testing period (and/or Harwood math teacher recommendation)
courses.notes: Designed to be taken concurrently with Integrated Math 2 in person.

courses.description: This course addresses math concepts including functions, trigonometry, and the real number system. These strands are unified by common themes and students will develop math habits of mind and interaction through a problem-based curriculum. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Function definition, notation, families, operations, transformations, and problem applications ●​ Use of circle and coordinate geometry to solve problems ●​ Trigonometric functions ●​ The real and complex number systems The goal of this course is to improve upon students' understanding of algebra and trigonometry with a special emphasis on families of functions and their transformations.
courses.prerequisites: Students must have a Proficient course score in Integrated Math 2

courses.description: Do you dream of being an independent, financially stable adult? This will be one of the most important courses you will ever take. This course introduces the fundamentals and skills of personal finance including budgeting, types of credit, managing credit, investments and savings. Use of the calculator and computer technology is emphasized. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Behavioral Finance ●​ Income & Taxes ●​ Banking: Checking & Savings ●​ Paying for College ●​ Types of Credit ●​ Managing Credit ●​ Investing ●​ Risk Management ●​ Budgeting The goal of this course is to introduce students to financial topics and to give students the skills to make thoughtful financial decisions now and in the future. Personal Finance for College Credit: For the 2026 fall semester, there will be the option to take this course for college credit. Students must meet all the class requirements as the student taking this course for Harwood credit plus the following: ●​ Use one of their dual enrollment vouchers ●​ Complete two independent learning units/projects on insurance and budgeting ●​ Answer additional questions on each of their three in-class summatives Students taking the class for college credit will be enrolled in the same PF classes as those taking it for Harwood credit. This is a great opportunity for students to use their dual enrollment vouchers for an in-person class without having to leave our campus!
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Math 1 OR Integrated Math 1 Online
courses.notes: For the 2026 fall semester there is an option to take this course for college credit using a dual enrollment voucher (details in description).

courses.description: Why is math important to you? How will it apply to your areas of interest and your future? Come explore these ideas in a project-based learning environment where you choose the math application that directly impacts you and the things you care about. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Math topics that are relevant to their interests ●​ Techniques and processes to solve complex scenarios ●​ Connections between different mathematical disciplines The goal of this course is for students to apply mathematical logic, problem solving techniques, and a variety of math content to solve applied problems. Students will see the relevance of math in their own lives!
courses.notes: Duration: Semester 1 Only

courses.description: This course is designed for students who plan to take Calculus at Harwood the following year. This course is a continuation of algebra and geometry topics required for the study of Calculus. Particular emphasis is given to topics that are fundamental to a first course in calculus including trigonometry, logarithms, function notation and transformation, and graphing calculator techniques. This class is a condensed and fast paced version of precalculus. Students can expect to: ●​ Increase fluency in interpreting math representations including tables, graphs, equations, situations ●​ Increase fluency in algebraic manipulation of equations ●​ Learn about applications and properties of Logarithms, Inverse functions, Rational Functions and Trigonometric Functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for Calculus or AP Calculus. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
courses.prerequisites: Students are currently enrolled in Integrated Math 3 and are maintaining a proficient score OR have completed Integrated Math 3 with a proficient course score
courses.notes: Duration: Semester 2 only

courses.description: This course is designed for students who have completed three experiences of Integrated Mathematics and are seriously interested in further exploration of mathematics. Throughout this course, students will continue to engage in mathematical habits of mind while gaining a deeper understanding of function behavior, algebraic modeling and manipulation. This course can serve as a prerequisite class for Calculus (either at Harwood or at college) or as an advanced math elective. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Transformations and manipulations of functions as related to the four mathematical representations of functions (graphical, tabular, algebraic, verbal) ●​ In depth analysis of the following types of functions: Trigonometric functions, Polynomials, Rational functions, Exponential functions, Logarithmic functions, and Inverse functions The goal of this course is to prepare students for further studies of mathematics, such as Calculus, as well as other college level maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3

courses.description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Generally, concepts are presented informally and intuitively as well as proven more formally. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral and Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I and Part II) The goal of this course is to prepare students for college level math classes. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus

courses.description: Do you want to be able to watch the news or read an article and understand what’s really going on? This course will teach you to develop critical thinking and analytic skills in order to act as an informed consumer. This course will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics may include: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses The goal of this course is to introduce students to the major concepts and tools for collecting, analyzing and drawing conclusions from data.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2

courses.description: This is a course in one-variable Calculus for college-bound students. The course includes graphical, numerical, and algebraic techniques of both derivation and integration. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Calculus course to prepare students to take the Calculus AB Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Calculus are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ The concept of a derivative and its applications ●​ How to find the derivative of most two variable functions ●​ The concept of an integral and its applications ●​ How to find the integral of most two variable functions ●​ The connection between Integral & Derivative Calculus (The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus Part I & II) ●​ Preparation for the AP Calculus Examination The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Calculus exam and other college maths. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 AND either Bridge to Calculus OR Precalculus; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework; If students are not proficient in AP Calculus by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Calculus.

courses.description: The AP course in statistics will introduce students to four broad conceptual themes of statistics: exploring data, sampling and experimentation, anticipating patterns, and making statistical inferences. Topics are covered at a faster pace than the other Statistics course to prepare students to take the Statistics Advanced Placement Exam in May. Students enrolling in AP Statistics are strongly encouraged to take the AP exam. Students can expect to learn about: ●​ Exploring and understanding data by describing patterns and departures from patterns ●​ Exploring relationships between variables ●​ Planning a study and gathering data ●​ Exploring randomness and probability ●​ Making inferences about situations by estimating population parameters and testing hypotheses ●​ Using inferences to determine when variables are related The goal of this course is to prepare students for the AP Statistics exam and provide a general understanding of statistical analysis. Graphing calculators are required and used extensively. We encourage students to have their own calculators but there are some available for loan from the math department if needed.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient course score in Integrated Math 3 OR Advanced score in Integrated Math 2.; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework.; If students are not proficient in AP Statistics by the end of Quarter 1, they will switch to regular Statistics.

courses.description: This performance-based class will study a variety of genres of music and participate in various concerts throughout the year. Together we will learn the fundamentals of music literacy, meaningful & expressive singing, and composition! All grades and experience levels are welcome. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for local, state, and regional music festivals, as well as an after-school honors choir.
courses.notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

courses.description: This course offers music students a large ensemble experience to build instrumental technique through the study and performance of varied musical styles including but not limited to contemporary concert band, 20th century rock, jazz, soul, funk, latin, experimental and film music. Performance skills, techniques, theory and varied music literature are explored. Students can expect to play concerts throughout the year and should have at least two years of reading music to enroll in this class. Students will also have the opportunity to audition for local, state, and regional music festivals. There is NO prerequisite for this course.
courses.notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

courses.description: This course is designed to create opportunities for students to engage in contemporary music performance both as a musician and/or crew member. The band regularly plays for school assemblies, community events, and various gigs in Vermont. Performing in the Assembly Band (guitar, bass, drums, keyboard, vocals, wind instrument) by teacher recommendation.
courses.notes: Department note: all music classes are available to students of all grades.

courses.description: In this year-long course, the primary charge is for students to build and operate a near-professional media production company that puts on a short production (assembly) every few weeks for the school community. Student tasks and responsibilities will vary depending on their particular job in the company. The jobs can be organized into the following categories: Pre-Production Staff and outreach: Script writer, social media manager, promotion, spirit committee, outreach Production Crew: Stage manager, stage crew, light design/operation, sound engineer, show hosts Film Crew: Camera operators, post-production editors
courses.notes: Duration: Year-Long ELO Series

courses.description: This course is designed for students who want to learn how to form their own band and develop a set of music. This is a great stepping stone for students who may ultimately perform in the assembly band. The course is open to vocalists and beginning to intermediate guitar, bass, keys and drum students. At the start of the semester, our focus will be on building technique through the learning of simple classic and modern rock songs. As we progress through the semester, we will explore original songwriting and how to craft our own arrangements of cover songs. The semester will culminate with a recording session and/or a live performance. Although welcome, no prior musical experience is required.
courses.notes: Duration: Semester-Long ELO Series

courses.description: This series approaches music theory through the lens of writing music. Intended for all students who are motivated to study music and interested in music, language, composition, technology, history, and performing.
courses.notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

courses.description: This series is designed for students interested in singing and performing contemporary vocal styles like pop, R&B, jazz, musical theater, rock, etc. All experience levels are welcome. Students will develop vocal technique through one-on-one and group instruction. Students will have opportunities to perform for each other as well as in the community.
courses.notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

courses.description: This series is for students interested in learning production techniques in electronic music. We will use a variety of music hardware and software to learn the art of DJing, and production, remixing, mashups, live looping, EDM, original composition, video game scoring. The experience will include a live performance/ presentation in the style of a DJ set and/or screening of their work. Although welcome, no prior musical experience is required, just an interest in producing, creativity and sharing new work.
courses.notes: Opt-in ELO series, offered as student interest and staff availability allows; no grades, length or prerequisites stated.

courses.description: This laboratory science course will engage students in learning about the formation of the universe and the earth. Students will start by learning about the universe including the atoms that make it up, the Big Bang theory, as well as stellar evolution and nuclear fusion. Students will then learn about the history of the earth starting with how the solar system was made, to how it is constantly changing, and how we are able to know the ages of things on earth. Lastly, students will learn about the history of life on earth and scientific innovations that have shaped our lives so far. The goal of this course is to provide students with a foundation of science skills and science knowledge by covering Next Generation Science Standards in earth science, life science, and physical sciences.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: This laboratory science course will engage students in learning about the different systems that play a part in our dynamic biosphere and atmosphere. We will focus on building our repertoire of science skills, including engineering design, reading informational texts, and designing experiments. Students will learn about energy, chemical reactions, cycles of matter, the oceans, the atmosphere, global climate change, and genetics. The goal of this course is to provide students with a foundation of science skills and science knowledge by covering Next Generation Science Standards in earth science, life science, and physical science.
courses.notes: Extended studies offered (Flexible Pathways: add-on in core 9th and 10th grade English, Science and Social Studies courses; no registration, opt in at start of course).

courses.description: Come learn about how scientific knowledge and scientific experiments play a role in our legal system. We will design and conduct experiments relating to different types of evidence and also learn about how those types of evidence can be used to help solve crimes. This course will also look into the limitations of using forensic science and how it has led to wrongful convictions. *This elective class runs every other year

Have you ever wondered why you do the things you do? What drives your emotions and behavior? In Science of the Mind students will study the adolescent brain and how it influences adolescents' interactions with the world. Students will have the opportunity to learn about the biological structure, function, and development of the adolescent brain. Throughout this learning, students will build connections between the biological and social influences that lead to their everyday social, emotional, biological experiences and well being. *This elective class runs every other year

Come learn about how living things work! Investigate the inner workings of cells that make up all living things. Zoom in on DNA, the molecule of inheritance, to discover its role in determining our genetic traits. Then look at the world's ecosystems to see how these cellular and molecular systems interact on a global scale. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Biology concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Biology.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
courses.fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Biology.

courses.description: Ready for some reactions? Come learn about the matter that makes up our world and how it relates to various phenomena such as oil spills and the Flint water crisis. This science laboratory course engages students in learning about what our world is made up of on the atomic and molecular level and how those particles interact with each other and change through chemical reactions. We will also learn mathematical applications that allow us to calculate the quantities of atoms and molecules in various substances and solutions, and learn how to model and explain various conceptual ideas relating to atoms, molecules and chemical reactions. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Chemistry concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of chemistry.
courses.prerequisites: Successful Completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
courses.fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of chemistry.

courses.description: Welcome to Physics! This course is designed as an algebra-based, introductory physics course where students look into the fundamental patterns of motion and forces. Students will learn about how the universe is governed by simple laws, which can be discovered through experimentation and graphical analysis. We will begin with the basics of motion and Newton’s Laws, and dive into energy and momentum. This laboratory course is designed to build upon the Physics concepts that are introduced in the Integrated Science courses. Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Physics.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2
courses.fulfills_text: Completing this course as well as integrated science 1 + 2 is equivalent to 1 year of Physics.

courses.description: Advanced Placement Biology is a college level Biology course. Students will learn how to apply biological knowledge, problem-solving skills, and scientific thinking that can be utilized to take the AP Biology test. During this course students will delve deeper into intricate biological details, move at an accelerated rate, while demonstrating independence and self-direction. Students who take the AP Biology course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Successful completion of or co-registration in Chemistry; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: How can we meet the needs of a growing population while sustaining natural resources? How can the global community collaborate to address environmental challenges? What does science tell us about our relationship with and dependence on the earth? In AP Environmental Science, you’ll cultivate your understanding of the interrelationships of the natural world through inquiry-based lab investigations and field work as you explore concepts like the four Big Ideas; energy transfer, interactions between earth systems, interactions between different species and the environment, and sustainability. Students who take the AP Environmental Science course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: Are you ready for an intellectually challenging and rigorous college level course? Students will be completing the equivalent curriculum to a general chemistry class at a college or university, therefore it is a very fast paced course. Strong math and reasoning skills are needed for success in this course. This course will also require a good work ethic with independent motivation for students to study and learn material outside of class. It is estimated that students will be expected to complete 1 hour of studying/work per night for this course. The course will run for two blocks, which will include laboratory time, lecture time, and group problem solving time. Students who take the AP Chemistry course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of Integrated Science 1 and 2; Completion of Integrated Math 2; Successful completion of OR Co-enrollment in Integrated Math 3; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework
courses.notes: Duration: Year-long, double block

courses.description: AP Physics 1 is an algebra based, college level Physics course. Students will cultivate their understanding of physics through inquiry based experimentation, in class Harkness discussions, textbook readings and online homework. The course covers topics of projectile motion, forces, energy, momentum, simple harmonic motion, and torque and rotation. Students who take the AP Physics course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.
courses.prerequisites: Successful completion of Integrated Science 1 & 2; Successful completion of Integrated Math 2; Successful completion of or co-enrollment in Integrated Math 3; Self-Assessment of AP Science Course Readiness; Students are expected to successfully complete the summer homework

courses.description: AP Computer Science Principles introduces students to the world of computer programming which has many applications in a variety of career fields. Working with your classmates to address real world problems, you will use your creativity to design and develop a computer program that collects and manages data using efficient algorithms. No previous coding experience is required. AP Computer Science Principles is equivalent to a first-semester college computing course. Students who take the AP Computer Science Principles course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam.

Principles of Engineering (POE) is a foundation course of Project Lead The Way (PLTW) engineering pathway for high schoolers. This course explores a variety of engineering concepts to help students determine a potential pathway in engineering following high school. Through problems that engage and challenge, students explore a broad range of engineering disciplines, including mechanisms, materials, structures, circuits, and programming. The course applies and concurrently develops secondary level knowledge and skills in mathematics, science, and technology culminating in a final robotics project.

Game Design is a project based course to explore the world of computer game development. The course begins with guided tutorials in a game engine. After acquiring the needed skills, students will build a unique game using the iterative design process. Throughout the course, we will explore the qualities of successful games along with the many facets of design and engineering used in video game development.

This course will serve as an introduction to computer programming with basic algorithms. Students will utilize the Python programming language to develop an understanding of concepts such as variables, functions, and control structures as they analyze, write, and test code. This class is for beginners; no programming experience is required.

Previously called Designing Sustainability, this course aims to help students develop an engineering mindset, which can be used to design and promote sustainable solutions to some of the world’s largest problems. Potential topics include water purification, energy and waste, growing food, and technology. Through the study of systems dynamics, change theory, and public policy, students will begin to better understand the complex interactions between our environment, economy, and society, and develop critical skill sets they can use to create a more just, joyful, and sustainable community. Completion of this course can count as a semester science experience.
courses.fulfills_text: Completion of this course can count as a semester science experience.

courses.description: This is a foundational art course with a focus on two-dimensional visual art (drawing, painting, and printmaking). Students will experiment with different art concepts and techniques, as well as many different materials. Each project allows students to personalize their work while engaging in the structure of new techniques/concepts/materials. *This is a prerequisite class for Art 2, Art for Harwood, and Advanced Studio Art.

This studio-based course introduces students to a variety of professional quality, functional artwork through experiencing a variety of traditional and nontraditional materials and methods. Students are encouraged to develop their own personal creativity and craftsmanship with hands-on projects. Projects are created with a variety of materials like clay, leather, and paper. *This is a prerequisite class for Pottery 1, Jewelry, and Ceramics

This class is a comprehensive introduction to software-based graphic design using Adobe Creative Suite. Successful advertising and design are instrumental in today’s multimedia-based economy. Learn the tools that professionals use in their day-to-day lives. Students dive into the elements of design, color theory, layout, text-based design, and image manipulation. Throughout the course, students will complete a diverse range of projects from logo designs, posters & magazine covers, to original low-poly portraits. The goal of this course is to become proficient in the elements and principles of design and Adobe Photoshop. *This is a prerequisite class for Digital Photography 1

Art 2 builds upon knowledge learned in Art I with an emphasis placed on: technical aspects of art creation and expressing ideas through a variety of styles and methods. This course is for students who want an opportunity to extend their understanding and skill development in the two-dimensional and even three-dimensional areas. *This is a prerequisite class for Art for Harwood, and Advanced Studio Art.

This class is for students who want to advance their personal development in the Digital Arts. Students who have successfully taken Graphic Design and Photo I (with a proficient score) are invited to dive deeper into the Digital Art world through a project-based environment that will enable greater freedom to explore, create, and find their own artistic voice. Using an individualized approach, students will work on projects based around Rebranding, Photo Restoration, Photojournalism, Commercial Photography, Marketing, and typography and fully exploring the interaction of text and image. This is a challenging and exciting class, which requires creative brainstorming, conceptualizing, critical thinking, collaboration, and presentation. The goal of this course is to gain confidence in your digital art skills as you advance your techniques while working with industry-standard equipment and programs.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient in Graphic Design and Digital Photography 1

courses.description: This course is an in depth exploration into clay, using various handbuilding techniques- pinch, slab and coil. Time is devoted to terminology, techniques, tools, and surface treatments, such as glazes and underglazes. All students cooperate in clay recycling as well as loading and unloading the kiln. Students are encouraged to develop their creativity and incorporate their own vision into each of their projects.

Advanced Studio Art is a course for independent students who want to strengthen their skills and experience in art. This offering is for students who (but not limited to): students who want to focus on a specific idea and/or medium, and/or students who want to develop a portfolio of their artwork for applying to college. This is a personalized course, therefore, students will work with the teacher on developing projects, setting goals, documenting work, taking part in class critiques and setting up the art show.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient in Art 1 and Art 2 OR Art 1 and permission from teacher

courses.description: This course introduces students to various processes of jewelry making. Students will be exploring materials such as wire, glass, clay and metal to create their designs. Students will create earrings, pendants, bracelets and rings from a variety of techniques and materials. Historical and contemporary processes will be explored with an emphasis on design and craftsmanship.

Learn the basics of the potter’s wheel, such as centering, opening, pulling, shaping and trimming vessels such as bowls, mugs and covered jars. Students assist in loading and unloading the kiln and complete all of their projects with glaze. Learn through step by step instructions and demonstrations. Individual creativity and development are encouraged through the creation of functional and decorative projects. *This is a prerequisite class for Pottery 2

This is an intensive course for students who are serious about their continued growth and experiences on the potter’s wheel. This class is a continuation of Pottery I and reviews basic information about clay, wheel throwing, glazes and kiln technology and expands on these skills and techniques. This course will focus on the student’s aesthetic and technical development in the creation of larger and more complex wheel-thrown functional pieces.

This comprehensive introduction to the photographic medium includes both the building of technical skills, as well as finding one’s creative voice in visual art. Students will learn how to manually photograph with school provided DSLR cameras, discover the Elements & Principles of photography, learn how to edit with top of the line editing software and print their finished work. Class projects will exhibit the unique and relevant vision that every student has as observers of the human experience. Students are also continually introduced to past and present artists as they begin to develop their own personal style and vision as a photographer. The goal of this course is to become proficient in digital photography through the understanding of: manual camera settings and functions, the elements and principles of design and how they contribute to successful photographs, editing, printing and critiquing your own work. *This is a prerequisite class for Digital Photography 2 & Advanced Digital Art

This continuation of Photography I enables students to further develop their personal vision in photography within a project-based learning environment. Having mastered the importance of the foundational processes in Photo I, this class enables students greater freedom to explore and create their own voice through advanced technical skills, collage, mixed media, and alternative processes. Students will also learn the critical skills needed to build a portfolio of multiple visual art pieces within personalized project design.
courses.prerequisites: Proficient in Graphic Design & Digital Photography 1

courses.description: This course is designed to provide students a basic introduction of skills and knowledge for the different ways one can be physically active for now and the future based on the classes that are offered here at Harwood: CardioWeight Training, Outdoor Adventure, Teaching Games for Understanding, Individual/Dual Activities, and Move & Groove. Students can expect to learn and experience the physical, social and emotional benefits of being physically active in different forms. Throughout the semester students will have the opportunity to learn, explore, and experience working individually, with partners, in small and large groups and how groups form and function based on the stages of group development. Using the activities implemented in class as evidence, students will report on the characteristics of each stage of group development (Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing and Adjourning). The goal of this course is to ensure all students have a solid base towards their physical literacy journey (introduction of all PE classes) while also building up on their social emotional learning skills (Reviewing the 5 stages of Group Dynamics) to help influence one’s communication skills within a group to enhance their ability to be active outside of school and moving forward as adults. This is the prerequisite class for students to then choose which class(es) they want a deeper level of skills and knowledge towards.
courses.prerequisites: This course is required in 9th grade before taking any other PE course.
courses.fulfills_text: This course is required in 9th grade before taking any other PE course.
courses.notes: Wellness chart lists it as "Foundations for Physical Education (PE)".

courses.description: Students will participate in single, partner and team activities through a Teaching Games for Understanding approach. Skills and Strategies will be broken down based on the category that the activity falls under. Games/Activities may include: ●​ Target Games - Archery, Disc Golf, Ball Golf, Bocce, Cornhole, Ladder Ball, Kan-Jam, Bowling. ●​ Net/Wall Games - Volleyball, Badminton, Pickleball, Table Tennis, Spikeball, Nitroball, Eclipseball ●​ Invasion Games - Flag football, Basketball, Floor Hockey, Flag Rugby, Ultimate Frisbee, Capture the Flag ●​ Striking and Fielding Games - Kickball, Wiffleball, Baseball/Softball, Cricket Activities offered will depend on weather, class enrollment and availability of facilities. Students will develop independent learning skills as well as team skills while supporting each other towards being physically active. They will also gain an understanding of lifetime activities and the influence games have on physical, social, and emotional health.

Students will participate in single/partner/small group activities such as archery, badminton, tennis, pickleball, table tennis, volleyball, golf, circus skills, disc golf, bowling, orienteering, snowshoeing, and lawn games. Activities offered will depend on weather, class enrollment and availability of facilities. Students will develop independent learning skills, cooperation with classmates, and an understanding of lifetime activities.

This course allows students to demonstrate forms of mindfulness, yoga, and dance. Course content might involve learning and participating in yoga sequences, meditations, and styles of ballroom dancing. Students will learn choreography and perform for others. Students will also choreograph their own piece.

Students get to experience the benefits of the great outdoors here on campus. Students will participate in outdoor activities and will learn about outdoor pursuits such as camping and survival skills, hiking skills, snowshoeing, sledding, archery, orienteering, trip planning and possibly more! Activities offered will depend on weather, class enrollment and availability of facilities. Students will develop independent learning skills and an understanding of lifetime activities.

Students will evaluate personal, family, community and global issues related to the concepts of wellness. Specific topics include: Substance Use, Nutrition, Stress and Mental Health, Violence Prevention, Relationships, Human Sexuality, Disease Prevention. Students will also be required to learn CPR.

Students will create a personal fitness goal with an emphasis on living an active and healthy lifestyle. The course content revolves around the students self designed personal fitness goal, involving heart rate monitoring, weight training, cardiovascular fitness, and flexibility/recovery exercises. Students will develop independent learning skills, and an understanding of lifetime fitness. Students will need to be intrinsically motivated as this class focuses on performing a range of fitness exercises every class and documenting information to highlight personal fitness gains.

Students will be introduced to fundamental skills, methods, and concepts relating to the field of coaching. Topics include adolescent development, group organization and management, coaching philosophies, and teaching of skills. Students are expected to apply their learning in school to a community setting, such as observing coaches at sports or other community events and reflecting on those experiences.

This course allows students to earn a PE credit by participating in athletics at Harwood Union High School. Students choosing this path will need to: ●​ Participate in two seasons of athletics to receive 1 semester P.E. opportunity. ●​ Students will receive a grade of SC (Successful Completion) for the sport season, as long as they have a grade of proficient or higher on all course assignments and have participated in a minimum of 80% of their sport season. ●​ The seasons can be different and the sports can be different ●​ Athletes are signed up to attend an ELO once teams are determined where they will be given a course introduction and registration information. Arrangements will be made for students who have conflicts with attending the ELO. ●​ It is the student’s responsibility to register following the steps provided ●​ Limit of 1 semester PE learning opportunity can be earned through this option toward graduation proficiencies for physical education.
courses.fulfills_text: This course allows students to earn a PE credit by participating in athletics at Harwood Union High School.
courses.notes: program; two seasons of athletics = 1 semester PE opportunity; limit of 1 semester PE learning opportunity through this option.

courses.description: This course will allow students to participate in one semester of PE through the Independent Study for Physical Education (IS-PE) course. A limited number of students can take this course. ●​ The course will be offered in the fall and spring semesters and over the summer. ●​ Students interested in participating in this opportunity should sign up with their School Counselor at the time you would complete your course registration for the next semester classes. ●​ Students will be assigned to an ELO early in the semester or just before the end of school for summer classes where they will be given a course introduction and registration information. Arrangements will be made for students who have conflicts attending the ELO. ●​ Limit of 1 semester PE learning opportunity can be earned through this option toward graduation proficiencies for physical education. ●​ Enrollment in this course is based on a first come first served basis with seniors given priority & juniors, then sophomores and freshmen. ●​ Seniors may only enroll in the summer or fall sections of the course.
courses.notes: program; limit of 1 semester PE learning opportunity through this option; offered fall, spring and summer; limited enrollment.

courses.description: In this course, students will be introduced to the major characters and stories of ancient Greek and Roman mythology. In doing so, students will explore such questions as: What is myth? Why do societies create myths? How does mythology shape thought and culture? Students will also analyze the legacy of classical myth in art, literature, film, and theater, from the plays of Shakespeare to the modern musical Hadestown. Throughout the course, building an argument, both in writing and in discussion, using literary and artistic evidence from our sources, will be emphasized.
courses.notes: Listed in the World Language section.

courses.description: In French 1, the emphasis is all about understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials .The main goal of this course is to learn the basics of the French language. Listening and speaking skills are a prime concern, thus the emphasis is on meaningful communication in everyday situations. Students practice grammar, vocabulary, and idioms orally and then have these skills reinforced in reading and writing. Students enjoy an introduction to the French-speaking world through slides, videos, storytelling, and discussion.

This is the second level of French offered at Harwood. The emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. It is a critical level, designed to increase the student’s fluency and confidence in the language through continued reading, vocabulary enrichment, listening, oral practice and cultural awareness. Students improve their speaking in French through role-playing everyday situations in both guided and open conversation as well as through direct dialogue. Both reading and listening comprehension are reinforced and expanded using different types of resources. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, songs, and cooking.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of French 1 or department approval
courses.notes: Chart: students who completed French 1 in 7th/8th grade begin with French 2 in 9th grade.

courses.description: In French 3, the emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. At the same time, students are also encouraged to grapple more with language patterns and grammatical structures, and apply them to their speech and writing. This can be a pivotal year which can encourage students to continue pursuing language study thanks to the curiosity and confidence it can provide, while pushing the rigorous demands of this level of language.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of French 2 or department approval

courses.description: At the fourth level of French offered at Harwood, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in French at an intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open. Their listening competency is addressed using various recordings and videos. Students improve their reading in French using authentic short stories (written and/or visual). Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations and songs, and hopefully penpal communication and visit?!
courses.prerequisites: Completion of French 3 or department approval

courses.description: At the fifth level of French, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in French at an upper-intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open, as well as through student-led Harkness discussions. Expectations are that French will be spoken 90%+ of the time. Emphasis is placed on discovering and analyzing current events. Students improve their reading in French using authentic sources and materials. Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations, song and cooking. Students who take the AP French course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam. *In addition, seniors will be eligible for the Seal of Biliteracy. The Seal of Biliteracy is an award given by the Vermont Organization of Classics and Language Educators under the authorization of the Agency of Education in recognition of students who have studied and attained proficiency in two or more languages [including English] by high school graduation. The Seal of Biliteracy takes the form of a seal that appears on the transcript or diploma of the graduating senior and is a statement of accomplishment for future employers and for college admissions. More information will be provided by World Language teachers.
courses.prerequisites: Completion of French 4 or department approval
courses.notes: One heading covering French 5 / AP / Seal of Biliteracy; seniors eligible for the Seal of Biliteracy.

courses.description: In Spanish 1, the emphasis is on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. The main goal of this course is to learn the basics of the Spanish language. Listening and speaking skills are a prime concern, thus the emphasis is on meaningful communication in everyday situations. Students practice grammar, vocabulary, and idioms orally and then have these skills reinforced in reading and writing. Students enjoy an introduction to the Spanish-speaking world through slides, videos, storytelling, and discussion.

In Spanish 2 the emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. Spanish II is a critical level, designed to increase the student’s fluency and confidence in the language through continued reading, vocabulary enrichment, listening and oral practice as well as continued awareness of Hispanic cultures. Storytelling remains an important aspect of the learning process. Students improve their speaking fluency by retelling stories, participating in role-playing activities, and giving oral presentations in Spanish. Both reading and listening comprehension are reinforced and expanded using different types of resources ranging from authentic reading materials, cultural movies in the target language, guest speakers and group discussions.
courses.notes: Chart: students who completed Spanish 1 in 7th/8th grade begin with Spanish 2 in 9th grade.

courses.description: In Spanish 3 the emphasis continues to be on understandable communication (what we call “comprehensible input”) from students, teacher(s), and course materials. Spanish III is a critical level, designed to increase the student’s fluency and confidence in the language through reading, vocabulary enrichment, listening, spoken and increased written practice. Storytelling remains an important aspect of the learning process. Students improve their speaking fluency by retelling stories both in writing and verbally. They will also participate in role-playing activities (murder mystery)and giving oral presentations in Spanish.

At the fourth level of Spanish, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in Spanish at an intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open. Their listening competency is addressed using recordings and videos of all types. Students improve their reading in Spanish using authentic short stories. Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations, song and cooking.

At the fifth level of Spanish, all areas of language competency are refined to make the students more comfortable communicating in Spanish at an upper-intermediate level. Methods of instruction are extremely diverse. Students improve their speaking skills through daily conversation, both thematic and open, as well as through student-led Harkness discussions. Emphasis is placed on discovering and analyzing current events. Students improve their reading in Spanish using authentic sources and materials. Writing abilities improve through the acquisition of more complex grammatical structures and tenses. Students also increase their cultural awareness through readings, presentations, song and cooking. Students who take the AP Spanish course are strongly encouraged to take the national exam. *In addition, seniors will be eligible for the Seal of Biliteracy.
